title: The 4am Chai Stop
dek: On a Himalayan road where the only thing open is a tin shed, and why that became the best part of the trip.
author: Pehchan Editorial

body.text: The driver stopped without asking. It was four in the morning, we were somewhere above Nako with the headlights making a small yellow room in front of us, and there was a tin shed with a bulb outside it. He turned off the engine, which is when I understood how loud the engine had been.

Inside, a man in three jackets was already boiling milk. Not for us — for himself, and for whoever came. This is the part of Himalayan road travel nobody photographs: the economy of small kindnesses that keeps a road open at four in the morning in a place where nothing else is.
What the guidebooks do not tell you about the driving days

Every itinerary for Spiti treats the driving as the cost of the destination. Eight hours to Sangla. Seven to Nako. Six to Kaza. The days are listed the way you list a customs queue — something to be endured on the way to the thing you came for.

This is wrong, and I think it is wrong in a way that matters beyond Spiti. The driving days are where the landscape actually changes. You do not arrive in the cold desert; you watch the pine give out somewhere past Reckong Peo and get replaced by nothing, and then by ochre, and then by a scale that stops making sense. If you sleep through it, you have paid for a landscape you did not see.
You do not arrive in the cold desert. You watch the pine give out and get replaced by nothing, and then by ochre.
The chai was not good

I want to be honest about this, because travel writing has a habit of improving things. It was oversweet, boiled long past the point of tea, and served in a glass that had been rinsed rather than washed. It was also the best thing I drank in eleven days, for reasons that have nothing to do with the tea.

We stood outside because the shed was too small for four people. The sky at 3,600 metres, with no moon and no town for forty kilometres, is not dark. It is crowded. Somebody said so, and then nobody said anything for about ten minutes, which on a trip with three other people is its own kind of achievement.
What I would do differently

I would build the stops in. Not the viewpoints — the viewpoints take care of themselves and are usually full of people doing the same calculation you are. I mean the unscheduled hour: leave two hours of slack in every driving day and spend it wherever the driver slows down without being asked. He knows. He has been doing this road for eleven years and he knows exactly where the good tin sheds are.
That is most of what I have learned about travelling in the mountains, and it took an oversweet glass of chai at four in the morning to work it out.

title: Eating Alone in Oaxaca
dek: Nine days of solo meals in a city where food is a communal act, and what the market taught me about being on my own.
author: Pehchan Editorial

body.text: The hardest table to ask for anywhere is a table for one at eight in the evening. In Oaxaca I stopped asking, and started eating standing up at the market, and the trip improved immediately.
The market solves the solo problem

Mercado 20 de Noviembre has a corridor of grills where you buy meat by weight, take it to a counter, and someone hands you tortillas and salsas without a conversation about whether anyone is joining you. You sit on a bench next to strangers doing exactly the same thing. Nobody is eating alone in a market. Everybody is eating alone in a market.

This is not a workaround. It is how a great deal of the city eats, and the food is not a lesser version of the restaurant food — in several cases it is the same cooks, cooking the thing they are best at, for a third of the money.
Seven moles is a marketing number

You will hear about the seven moles constantly. It is a real tradition and also a tidy figure that suits a menu. What I found more interesting was that every family cooks negro differently, and that asking about the difference is the single most reliable way to start a conversation in this city.
Nobody is eating alone in a market. Everybody is eating alone in a market.
On mezcal, and drinking alone

Mezcal is agricultural. An espadín takes six to eight years in the ground before anyone distils it; a tobalá can take considerably longer, and it does not grow in rows. Once you know that, the bar-shot version stops making sense and you start sipping it at room temperature, which is what everyone here does anyway.
A palenque day is also the easiest way to meet people if you have gone quiet. You share a van with six strangers, you all taste the same thing, and by the second stop somebody has opinions.
What nine days alone was actually like

Better than I expected, and boring in the middle, which I now think is the point. Days four and five of any solo trip are flat. You have exhausted the novelty and not yet arrived at the rhythm. If you can push through without booking a tour to fill the silence, day six is usually when the trip becomes yours.

title: What the Tea Estate Taught Me About Slow Mornings
dek: Three days on a working plantation above Munnar, and the argument for staying still.
author: Pehchan Editorial

body.text: The pluckers were already out when I got to the verandah at half past six, moving across a hillside in a line that from a distance looked like weather crossing the slope. I had come to Munnar with a list of six things to do and by the second morning I had done none of them.
The mist has a schedule

It comes up the valley from the south between six and seven, fills everything below fifteen hundred metres, and burns off by nine. If you leave for Eravikulam at seven you drive through it and see nothing. If you sit on a verandah with a cup of what was growing outside forty-eight hours earlier, you watch a valley disappear and come back.
This is not a profound observation. It is a scheduling one, and scheduling is most of what separates a good trip from a rushed one.
I had come with a list of six things to do and by the second morning I had done none of them.
A working estate is not a resort

The bungalow I stayed in has six rooms and about two thousand acres of tea around it, and the tea is the business — the rooms are the sideline. That changes what the staff know. The man who took me walking at dawn had been on that estate for nineteen years and could tell me which sections were replanted in the nineties by the colour of the leaf.
You cannot buy that in a hotel with a spa. It is worth choosing for, and it is worth paying for, and it is one of the few things in travel where the premium buys something real.
The case for three nights in one place

Two nights is one full day. Three nights is two full days plus a morning you do not have to plan, and that unplanned morning is reliably the one you remember. On a two-week trip that means five stops instead of eight. You will see less. You will have been somewhere.

title: The Hotel That Does Not Photograph Well
dek: Why the best places to stay are often the ones with no wide-angle shot, and how to find them.
author: Pehchan Editorial

body.text: The best room I have stayed in this year is four and a half tatami mats, has a window onto a courtyard the size of a parking space, and is impossible to photograph. There is nowhere to stand.
The wide-angle problem

Hotels are now designed for a camera at chest height in the corner of the room. That is a real design constraint and it produces real consequences: rooms that are wide rather than deep, beds facing the view rather than the wall, freestanding baths placed where they photograph rather than where you would want to sit in one.

A machiya townhouse cannot compete on this and does not try. Its pleasures are sequential — you come through a dark entrance, past a garden you did not expect, up a staircase that is too steep, into a room where the light comes through a wooden lattice and moves across the floor for about forty minutes in the late afternoon. None of that survives a single frame.
Its pleasures are sequential. None of that survives a single frame.
How to find them anyway

Read the one-star and three-star reviews rather than the five-star ones. The complaints tell you the shape of the place: 'stairs too steep', 'walls thin', 'no lift', 'small pool'. Those are the fingerprints of an old building that was converted rather than constructed, which is usually what you want.
Look at the room count. Under fifteen rooms means the person at the desk can actually book you a table. Over eighty and you are in a system.

And look for what the property does other than accommodate you. A working lemon terrace, a functioning tea estate, a family that has weaving looms in the back. The stay is better when the hotel is not the whole business.
The disclosure
We write about stays we would book ourselves, and we say plainly when a link earns us a commission. That does not make our judgement perfect. It should make it legible.

title: Nobody Tells You About the Wind
dek: Patagonia in photographs is still. Patagonia in person is not, and it changes everything about how you plan.
author: Pehchan Editorial

body.text: Four days in El Chaltén and I saw Fitz Roy for about ninety minutes total. That is not a complaint; it is the base rate. The people who come back with the photograph are the ones who stayed long enough to be there on the right morning.
Plan for the weather window, not the itinerary

Everywhere else you plan a route and hope the weather cooperates. Here you plan a set of options and pick one at six in the morning based on the forecast. The lodge posts it in the common room. Everyone reads it at breakfast and the village reorganises itself accordingly.

Which means a four-day stay is not four days of walking. It is two or three days of walking and one or two of reading, and if you have booked a tight schedule you will burn a weather window sitting on a bus.
You plan a set of options and pick one at six in the morning.
The wind is a real hazard, not an atmosphere

On the final section up to Laguna de los Tres, gusts come over the ridge with enough force to move you sideways. People turn back there, and they are right to. The mountain is not going anywhere and the trail is free — you can come back tomorrow, which is the underrated advantage of a place that requires no permit.
What to do with a blown-out day

Walk to Chorrillo del Salto, which takes an hour and is sheltered. Or do the lower Laguna Capri section and turn around at the treeline. Or, genuinely, do nothing: El Chaltén has a bakery, three good places to eat, and a common room culture built around people waiting for weather. Some of the best conversations I had on that trip happened on the days I did not walk.

title: The Riad and the Hard Sell
dek: On navigating Marrakech's commercial pressure without deciding the city is against you.
author: Pehchan Editorial

body.text: Within twenty minutes of entering the medina I had been told the square was closed, that the tanneries were open only today, and that the road I was walking down led nowhere. All three were false, delivered pleasantly, and are a standard opening.
It is a transaction, not an ambush

The framing most visitors arrive with — that this is hostility — makes the trip worse and is not accurate. Marrakech has a commission economy. Someone who redirects you to a shop earns a percentage. That is a job, and it is legal, and it is aimed at a very large number of visitors who arrive for two nights and will never come back.
Understanding it as an economic system rather than a personal one changes your response from irritation to a polite, repeatable no. Which is the only response that works.
Understanding it as an economic system rather than a personal one changes your response from irritation to a polite, repeatable no.
The three things that actually helped
First: book a riad that meets you at the taxi drop. The last four minutes on foot with luggage is where most bad first impressions are manufactured, and any decent riad will send someone.

Second: do a craft walk on day one with a guide from a medina family, explicitly with no commission stops. You learn the geography of the trades — dyers here, metal there — and after that the souks stop being a maze and start being a map.
Third: buy from the workshop, not the shopfront. The price is often similar and the difference in what reaches the maker is large.
What the city gives back

On the fourth evening, on a rooftop in the northern medina with the Atlas visible and snow on it, the muezzins started across the city at slightly different moments, the way they do. Nobody was selling me anything. That is the version of Marrakech that people come back for, and you have to get through the first afternoon to reach it.

title: A Week of Not Booking Anything
dek: An experiment in arriving in Hoi An with a bicycle, no reservations and no plan.
author: Pehchan Editorial

body.text: The rule was one booking: seven nights in a twelve-room house on the wrong side of the river. Everything else had to be decided that morning, on a bicycle, in a town small enough that this is not reckless.
What happens on day two

You get bored, and boredom is the mechanism. Without a schedule I cycled to the herb village because it was the direction I had not been in, ended up in a conversation about basil varieties with a woman who has grown them her whole life, and stayed for two hours. No tour would have allocated two hours to basil.
You get bored, and boredom is the mechanism.
The things you should still book

Cooking classes fill. Tailors need fitting appointments and lead time. The lantern full-moon nights fill every room in town. Unbooking works for the middle of a trip, not for the edges and not for the things with capacity limits.
Where it fails

It fails in high season, it fails anywhere with a permit system, and it fails if you have four days rather than eight. It also fails if you are the kind of traveller who will spend the unplanned morning on your phone researching what you should be doing — in which case book the trip and enjoy it, which is a legitimate way to travel and not a lesser one.
But in a flat town with a bicycle and a week, it produced the best trip I had that year, and the only itinerary I could write for it afterwards would have ruined it.

title: The Conservancy Difference
dek: Two safari camps, forty minutes apart, and why the boundary line between them changes the entire experience.
author: Pehchan Editorial

body.text: On the reserve side, we counted fourteen vehicles at a leopard. On the conservancy side, forty minutes north, the rule is five, and on the morning we found a cheetah with cubs there were two — ours and one other, which left after fifteen minutes.
What the boundary actually is

The Maasai Mara National Reserve is government land with open access for any licensed vehicle. The conservancies bordering it are private leases: Maasai landowning families lease their land to a small number of camps, which pay per bed per night, and in exchange the land carries a strict cap on vehicles and beds.
That single structural difference produces almost everything visitors notice. Vehicle limits at sightings. Permission to drive off-road, at night, and to walk. Fewer beds across a larger area.
On the reserve side we counted fourteen vehicles at a leopard. On the conservancy side, the rule is five.
The honest trade-off

Conservancy camps cost more, sometimes considerably. And the famous Mara river crossings are in the reserve, not the conservancies — so migration-season visitors usually need to drive in for those, which means joining the crowd for a morning.

There is also a fair argument that the reserve's open access is more democratic, and that a model where exclusivity is the product deserves scrutiny rather than automatic praise. The counter-argument is the payment structure: conservancy leases put money directly into the hands of the families who own the land, monthly, whether or not the beds are full.
What I would book

Three nights in a conservancy and one long day into the reserve during migration season. Outside migration season, all conservancy. And I would ask any camp, directly, what proportion of the nightly rate reaches the landowners — the good ones answer immediately.
